title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: §38 (previous page) claims that for every prime P there is a number a whose powers 1, a, a^2, … reduced mod P run through all P−1 nonzero residues; that is, a has multiplicative order P−1. The argument uses §21 (the order divides P−1) and §34 (x^{P−1}−1 has 'proper' cases x=a that divide no lower x^n−1). This Scholion (§39) illustrates the result.

The table gives the complete cycle of residues of a^k mod p for p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. The bases are a = 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 5 respectively. Euler notes that the base need not be printed separately, because it equals the second term of each row. The header row a^0, a^1, … lets the reader read off the exponent (in modern terms, the index or discrete logarithm) of each residue.

Euler then names such bases 'radices primitivae' (primitive roots): their powers give all distinct residues below the divisor before 1 recurs. He adds two remarks:
(i) No method is yet known for finding a primitive root for an arbitrary prime.
(ii) His existence proof is non-constructive; it does not show how to find one.

The next page says that in practice one finds a primitive root by trial. Take p=23: 2 has order 11, so one searches among the residues not reached by 2, and 5 works. §40 then proves a^{(p−1)/2} ≡ −1 for a primitive root a.
errors: This page has no logical error. The existence proof it relies on (§§34, 38) was later judged incomplete; Gauss (Disquisitiones, art. 56) noted that Euler's demonstration was insufficient and gave his own. This gap belongs to the preceding sections, not to this Scholion.

ideas.what: Naming of 'radix primitiva' for a base generating all nonzero residues mod a prime
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (term introduced in E449, 1774); existence proved rigorously by Gauss 1801 (Legendre also gave a proof)
ideas.where_published: E449, Opuscula analytica I (1783); discussed in Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History

ideas.what: Table of power residues / exponents for primes up to 23
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (indices, Disquisitiones art. 57ff., with a table), Jacobi Canon Arithmeticus 1839

ideas.what: Remark that no method is known to find primitive roots and that the existence proof is non-constructive; trial search in practice
ideas.modern_name: algorithmic problem of finding a primitive root (no unconditional deterministic polynomial-time algorithm known)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss's remark (Disquisitiones art. 73) that primitive roots are found by trial; modern computational number theory

missed.claim: Euler explicitly separates proving existence from having a method of finding the object. This is an early, articulate statement of a constructive/non-constructive distinction for primitive roots, anticipating Gauss's art. 73 and the modern algorithmic open problem. It is occasionally noted by historians but rarely credited.
missed.quote: neque etiam demonstratio, qua tales radices primitiuas semper dari euici, methodum eas inueniendi declarat.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Finding a primitive root deterministically in polynomial time remains open without GRH, so Euler's remark identifies a problem that is still unsolved. It is mainly of historiographic interest.

deep.surprise_reason: The coinage of 'primitive root' in E449 and its residue table are well known (Weil, Dickson's History). The table is correct and routine. The constructivity remark is noteworthy but already documented.
transcription_corrections: Row 11: the image prints '8, 5 10' without a comma between 5 and 10; the transcription correctly reads 5, 10.
Row 23: after 14 the image shows only '| etc.' with no repeated terms, which matches the transcription.
